questions.q: Why is a single suspicious transaction hard to catch with relational, row-by-row analysis?
options: Fraud rings deliberately spread activity across many accounts to avoid tripping simple per-account thresholds, so the signal is in the connection structure, not any one row
Relational databases cannot store transaction data at all
Fraud never involves more than one account, so graph analysis is unnecessary
SQL Server has no way to store numeric transaction amounts
questions.explain: The lesson explains that fraud rings spread activity to stay under per-account thresholds, which is why structural, graph-native analysis catches what row-level checks miss.

questions.q: In the graph fraud-detection pattern, what role does community detection play?
options: It finds clusters of accounts that transact heavily with each other but rarely connect to the broader legitimate network — the structural signature of a coordinated ring
It calculates the exact dollar amount lost to fraud
It encrypts transaction data between accounts
It replaces the need for any account authentication
questions.explain: Community detection surfaces the dense, insular clusters characteristic of coordinated fraud rings.

questions.q: Why does centrality matter specifically *within* a suspicious community, rather than across the whole graph?
options: A node with unusually high centrality inside a suspicious cluster is a stronger signal of a ring organizer or mule account than either community membership or centrality alone
Centrality only works when computed on the entire graph, never on a subset
Centrality inside a community always equals zero by definition
This combination has no practical benefit over using either technique alone
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this combination — centrality within an already-suspicious community — as a stronger signal than either metric used independently.

questions.q: In the recommendation engine pattern, why is node similarity typically computed offline rather than at request time?
options: Because similarity computation is expensive, so precomputing it and writing it as SIMILAR_TO relationships keeps the request-time query a cheap, fast traversal
Because Cypher cannot express similarity computations at all
Because offline computation produces less accurate results, which is preferred for privacy
Because SIMILAR_TO relationships cannot be queried with MATCH
questions.explain: This is the same offline-precompute, online-traverse pattern covered in the previous lesson — it keeps request-time latency low.

questions.q: What underlying reason does this lesson give for why graph databases work well for both fraud detection and recommendations?
options: The meaningful signal is in the shape of the connections around a node, not in that node's attributes alone, and graphs represent that shape natively
Both use cases require encrypting all data at rest
Both use cases are impossible to implement in any other type of database
Graph databases are simply faster at every type of query than relational databases
questions.explain: The lesson's closing point is that the structural, connection-based signal is what graphs represent natively, which is why they excel at both use cases.
